 Skydance CEO David Ellison onstage at the NYT Dealbook Summit on Nov 18, 2026 
 Getty 
 David Ellison covered a lot of ground and jumped over some landmines today at the New York Times Dealbook summit, but things got positively testy when it came to the topic of a federal tax credit for film and television.
 “When you look at who this incentive helps, the misnomer out there is you’re giving Tom Cruise a tax break,” the Skydance CEO told the power crowd packed into Lincoln Center on Wedbesday. “That’s not true.”
 Pushing back on host Andrew Ross Sorkin ‘s claim that lucrative tax credits do little to produce “measurable gains in jobs, wages, and economic growth,” Ellison insisted that a lot of his much battered relationship with Donald Trump and MAGA has been about getting a national plan in place as it has been about seeing his acquisition of Paramount and his $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery closed. As the bipartisan incentive initiative appears to be stalling in the lame duck Congress, Ellison cited stats from not just Canada, the UK and Australia on the usefulness of tax credits to attracting production and creating jobs, but also noted the return on investment previously solid red Texas has seen in recent years.

 In the end, just like in incentives rich California, New York and Georgia, its the unusually verbose Ellison says it’s ultimately not about the Mission Impossible star, but all about the economy stupid. 
 Watch on Deadline 
 “Tom Cruise, the biggest talent in the world, are going to get paid whatever they get paid, no matter where they shoot in the world,” Ellison bluntly and practically stated. “It is the union workers, it is the makeup artists, it is the craftsmen, it is the set builders that fundamentally are being subsidized. 
 “You are creating jobs.”
 Sending a message not just to Sorkin, but knowingly addressing to a Skydance suspicious and ailing American industry that has seen double digit production declines in L.A. and over 50,000 jobs lost over the past six years, the newly minted people’s prince clearly had a mission with the topic of tax credits. After facing down a blue state antirust suit and guild concerns to make Para and WBD one, Ellison is now seeking to defang worries around town and in Manhattan that he is primarily a tech-bro exec only interested in cutting and firing his way out of corporate debt 
 “You are helping small businesses, and every other country that has done this in the past does it because it is economically sustainable,” Ellison declared of the strength of a 25% credit program from DC that he sys he has been working behind the scenes for over the past year. “We think it is important that the United States does it because it is economically sustainable.” 
 In many ways, past Joe Biden donor Ellison, who made sure to brandish his bipartisan spurs over and over today in NYC, was loudly singing from the same choir book as traditional rivals Trump, Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) and the outgoing and incoming governor of California. 
 (L-R) Donald Trump, Gov. Gavin Newsom 
 Getty Images 
 Listing off supporters of the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, Trump trumpeted the measure on social media on November 13. “Everyone feels strongly about the Motion Picture and Television Industry — and so do I, and we all want to save it,” the former Apprentice host posted as the nation saw the FAA ground all flights for several hours over an alleged glitch. 
 One hold up to the MPTER Act moving forward currently is that the Joint Committee on Taxation yet to release its estimate of what it could cost. That report is necessary for any financial legislation to get to a vote in Congress. Throwing some cold water on the whole thing from outside Capitol Hill, the Cato Institute recently projected a national tax credit program could cost between $33 billion and $49 billion, That’s some big numbers to bandy about in an era of divided government. 
 Set to leave office in January and be succeed by Xavier Becerra, Gavin Newsom earlier this month proposed hiking the Golden State’s industry tax incentive to a capped $1 billion. If passed by the legislature in Sacramento once Becerra takes over, the rise in California’s tax credits would come just under a year and a half after the state’s program was raised from $330 million annually to $750 million .
 During the campaign, both Becerra and GOP gubernatorial rival Steve Hilton laid out proposals of their own to make the state’s film and TV tax credits program more competitive. Also, a first steps $10 million, post-production tax credit was signed into law by Newsom in September. 
 In the home of Hollywood itself, now Mayor-elect Nithya Raman had industry revitalization at the heart of her City Hall bid. To that, in a sign of real politick in action, the soon-to-be ex Councilmember and then candidate offered an olive branch to Ellison with the success of the Para-WBD deal. “To David Ellison, to his co-CEO, I don’t just want those dollars that you’ve committed to productions to be spent in America — I want them to be spent in Los Angeles,” the self-described industry “relentless advocate” and spouse of TV comedy scribe Vali Chandrasekaran said on October 1. 
 As, they say, hooray for Hollywood, hopefully.
